  Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds

Vignette:
# Marcus

Marcus was twenty-one when he enlisted, drawn by the promise of structure and purpose that his civilian life in rural Pennsylvania had never offered. He completed basic training and deployed to Afghanistan with the 101st Airborne Division in the spring of his second year of service. For the first months, the work was routine—patrols, checkpoints, the grinding monotony of vigilance in a landscape that looked nothing like home. Then, in late summer, his unit was tasked with clearing a compound suspected of housing insurgent materials. Marcus was part of the entry team.

What happened next arrived in his mind not as a coherent sequence but as a collection of sensory shards that his brain refused to stitch together. There was the smell—acrid, chemical, burnt—that filled his nose and throat as they moved through the first room. There was a sound, enormous and close, that he later understood was an IED detonating beneath the floorboards of the adjacent corridor. He remembered the shock wave, the way his body lifted and fell. He remembered the smell again, thicker now, mixed with something else. Two soldiers died in that corridor. Marcus was pulled out with a concussion and a fractured radius. He was medevaced, treated, and after six weeks of recovery, cleared to return to duty.

He did return, but something had fractured in him that the doctors could not see on a scan. The sound of the explosion lived in his nervous system. His body had learned to expect danger in specific ways, and now those ways were everywhere. When he was discharged honorably fourteen months later, he carried that learning home with him.

Back in the States, Marcus took work as a bus driver for the county transit system—a job that seemed stable, undemanding, a way to rebuild some version of normalcy. But the job placed him in direct contact with his triggers in ways he had not anticipated. The diesel engine of the bus, when it backfired or stalled, produced a sharp bang that sent his heart into his throat and his hands trembling on the wheel. The smell of burnt rubber or overheated brakes filled the cabin, and he found himself gripping the steering wheel so hard his knuckles went white, his breath shallow, his mind suddenly back in that compound. Worst of all were the helicopters. The county airfield was only three miles from his regular route, and several times a week, military transport helicopters passed low overhead. When Marcus heard that sound—the distinctive thump-thump-thump of rotor blades—he had to pull over. His vision would narrow. His hands would shake. Once, a passenger asked if he was all right, and Marcus found that he could not explain it. He knew what had happened to him, but the words simply would not come. There was no way to describe to a concerned stranger why a helicopter sound made him feel like he was dying.

By autumn, Marcus had begun to avoid the routes that passed near the airfield. He called in sick on days when he knew the flight schedule was heavy. The smell of crowds—the shopping mall, the farmer's market downtown, the church his mother still attended—became unbearable. He stopped going to Mass, stopped meeting friends at the bar, stopped doing anything that required him to be around people or to be unprepared for sudden noise. Instead, he spent his evenings in his apartment with his phone, scrolling through games and videos for hours, his mind numbed and occupied by anything that was not memory.

The memories themselves came in fragments that refused to cohere. He could isolate the smell, the sound, the pressure in his chest, but when he tried to think about the sequence of events, his mind fractured. The pieces did not connect. It was as though his brain had broken the experience into components and then locked them in separate rooms. This terrified him more than anything else—the sense that he could not hold the story of what happened to him in his mind as a single, comprehensible thing.

Over the winter, Marcus's supervisor began to ask questions about his absences. His mother called more frequently, worried about his isolation. He had stopped answering. What frightened him most was the thought that the world was fundamentally unsafe, that danger was not an anomaly but the baseline condition of existence, and that he was the only one awake to it. The hypervigilance was exhausting—the constant scanning, the need to know where exits were, which sounds were normal and which were threats. He was certain that if he lowered his guard for even a moment, something catastrophic would happen. He was equally certain that his life was not worth the effort it took to maintain that vigilance. In January, after three weeks without going to work, Marcus finally called a Veterans Affairs clinic and asked for help.
